# Risk Models {#risk-models}

## Short-Term Risk Models

Consider an insurance portfolio over a fixed time interval, such as one year.

The total amount paid in claims is uncertain because of two sources of randomness:

1. **Claim frequency:** how many claims occur.
2. **Claim severity:** how much each claim costs.

For example, a motor portfolio may produce 800 claims in one year and 950 in another. The individual claim amounts can also vary substantially.

The collective risk model combines these two sources of uncertainty into a model for the **aggregate claim amount**.

::: {.callout-note}

## Key idea

**Frequency + severity $\longrightarrow$ aggregate claims**

:::

---

## Frequency and Severity

Define the following random variables:

* $N$: number of claims during the fixed time interval;
* $X_i$: amount of the $i$th claim;
* $S$: total amount of claims.

The claim frequency is a discrete random variable,

$$
N\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.
$$

The claim severities $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ describe the amounts of individual claims.

For example, $N$ may have a Poisson distribution, while $X_i$ may have a Gamma, Lognormal, or Pareto distribution.

---

## Aggregate Claim Amount

If exactly $n$ claims occur, the total claim amount is

$$
S=X_1+\cdots+X_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i.
$$

But the number of claims is itself random. Therefore,

$$
\boxed{S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i}.
$$

The random variable $S$ is called the **aggregate loss**, **aggregate claim amount**, or **total claim amount**.

The number of terms in the sum is random because $N$ is random.

<!-- ::: {.callout-important} -->
<!-- ## Collective risk model -->

<!-- The number of terms in the sum is random because $N$ is random. -->
<!-- ::: -->

---

## Collective Risk Model Visual Guide



![](../figures/Collective_Risk_Model_Visual_Guide.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}



---

## Why Is $S$ a Random Sum?

The definition

$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i
$$

covers different numbers of claims:

$$
\begin{aligned}
N=0 &\Rightarrow S=0, &
N=1 &\Rightarrow S=X_1,\\
N=2 &\Rightarrow S=X_1+X_2, &
N=n &\Rightarrow S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the collective risk model is a **random sum model**. The aggregate loss depends on both the **number of claims** and their **sizes**.


---

## Assumptions of the Collective Risk Model

The standard collective risk model assumes:

1. The claim severities are independent and identically distributed:

   $$
   X_1,X_2,\ldots \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} F_X.
   $$

2. The claim frequency is independent of all claim severities:

   $$
   N\perp\!\!\!\perp (X_1,X_2,\ldots).
   $$

The first assumption gives all claims the same distribution and makes different claim amounts independent.

The second assumption means that the number of claims provides no information about their individual sizes.

---

## Interpretation of the Assumptions

These assumptions make the aggregate loss mathematically tractable.

In practice, they may not always hold.

For example:

* claim frequency and severity may be dependent;
* claims from the same event may be dependent;
* different types of claims may have different severity distributions.

The assumptions are therefore a **starting model** rather than a statement that all insurance portfolios behave exactly this way.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Modelling assumptions

$$
\boxed{
X_1,X_2,\ldots\text{ are iid},
\qquad
N\text{ is independent of }X_1,X_2,\ldots
}
$$

Always check whether these assumptions are reasonable for the application.
:::

---

## From Collective Risk Model to Compound Distribution

Under the standard assumptions, $S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i$

has a **compound distribution**.

The model can be viewed as two probability models combined:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Frequency model}
+
\text{Severity model}
\longrightarrow
\text{Aggregate loss model}
}
$$

The distribution chosen for $N$ determines the type of compound distribution.

| Frequency distribution | Aggregate distribution     |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Binomial               | Compound Binomial          |
| Poisson                | Compound Poisson           |
| Negative binomial      | Compound Negative Binomial |

---

## Why Study the Collective Risk Model?

The distribution of

$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i
$$

can, in principle, be obtained using convolution methods.

However, compound distributions generally do not have simple closed-form distributions.

For this reason, we focus on quantities that can be derived more easily, particularly:

* $E[S]$, the expected aggregate loss;
* $\operatorname{Var}(S)$, the variance of aggregate loss;
* important special compound distributions.

These results provide useful measures of the expected cost and variability of an insurance portfolio.

---

## Actuarial Applications

Once the aggregate loss model has been specified, it can be used to study:

* expected total claims; variability of total claims;
* probabilities such as $\Pr(S>x)$; reinsurance arrangements;
* premium calculations; capital and risk measures.

The collective risk model provides a common framework for combining claim frequency and claim severity.

::: {.callout-note}

## Key idea

The central model is

$$
\boxed{S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i}.
$$

The next step is to determine the **mean and variance of this random sum**.
:::



# Conditional Expectation and Variance

## Conditional Expectation and Variance Formulas

Conditional expectation and variance allow us to analyse a random variable by first conditioning on another random variable.

The **law of total expectation** is

$$
\boxed{E[E[X\mid Y]]=E[X]}.
$$

The **law of total variance** is

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=
E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]
+
\operatorname{Var}(E[X\mid Y])
}.
$$

These formulas will be used to analyse the aggregate loss

$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i.
$$

---

## Conditional Variance

The conditional variance of $X$ given $Y$ is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)
=
E\left[(X-E[X\mid Y])^2\mid Y\right].
$$

An equivalent expression is

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)
=
E[X^2\mid Y]-(E[X\mid Y])^2
}.
$$

The law of total variance then gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=
\underbrace{E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]}_{\text{variation within groups}}
+
\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(E[X\mid Y])}_{\text{variation between groups}}.
$$

---

## Conditional Expectation and Variance Formulas

![](../figures/The_Collective_Risk_Model_Overview.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}



---

## Example: Conditional Claim Amounts

An insurer classifies policyholders into three risk groups:

$$
Y\in\{L,M,H\},
\qquad
P(L)=P(M)=P(H)=\frac13.
$$

Conditional on the risk group, two claim amounts are equally likely.

| Risk group   | Claim amounts (THB) |
| ------------ | ------------------: |
| Low ($L$)    |               $1,2$ |
| Medium ($M$) |               $1,5$ |
| High ($H$)   |              $1,10$ |

Let $X$ denote the claim amount of a randomly selected policyholder.

---

## Example: Conditional Claim Amounts

**Questions**

1. Find the distribution of $X$.
2. Find $E[X]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
3. Verify the results using conditional expectation and variance.


---

## Distribution of the Claim Amount

The possible claim amounts are

$$
X\in\{1,2,5,10\}.
$$

For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X=1)
&=\sum_{y\in\{L,M,H\}}P(X=1\mid Y=y)P(Y=y)\\
&=\frac12\left(\frac13+\frac13+\frac13\right)
=\frac12.
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
P(X=2)=P(X=5)=P(X=10)=\frac16.
$$

---

## Distribution of the Claim Amount

Therefore, the probability distribution of $X$ is

| $x$      |       $1$ |       $2$ |       $5$ |      $10$ |
| -------- | --------: | --------: | --------: | --------: |
| $P(X=x)$ | $\frac12$ | $\frac16$ | $\frac16$ | $\frac16$ |


---

## Direct Calculation of the Mean

Using the distribution of $X$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X]
&=1\left(\frac12\right)
+2\left(\frac16\right)
+5\left(\frac16\right)
+10\left(\frac16\right)\\
&=\frac{10}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{E[X]=\frac{10}{3}}.
$$

---

## Direct Calculation of the Variance

First calculate the second moment:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X^2]
&=1^2\left(\frac12\right)
+2^2\left(\frac16\right)
+5^2\left(\frac16\right)
+10^2\left(\frac16\right)\\
&=22.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(X)
&=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2\\
&=22-\left(\frac{10}{3}\right)^2\\
&=\frac{98}{9}.
\end{aligned}
$$

<!-- Therefore, -->

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{98}{9}}. -->
<!-- $$ -->

---

## Conditional Means

Let $Y$ denote the risk group.

For the three groups,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X\mid L]&=\frac{1+2}{2}=\frac32,\\
E[X\mid M]&=\frac{1+5}{2}=3,\\
E[X\mid H]&=\frac{1+10}{2}=\frac{11}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the law of total expectation,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X]
&=E[E[X\mid Y]]\\
&=\frac13\left(
\frac32+3+\frac{11}{2}
\right)=\frac{10}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This agrees with the direct calculation.

---

## Conditional Variances

For two equally likely values $a$ and $b$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=
\frac{a^2+b^2}{2}
-\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X\mid L)=\frac14,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X\mid M)=4,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X\mid H)=\frac{81}{4}.
$$

The average within-group variation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]
&=\frac13\left(
\frac14+4+\frac{81}{4}
\right) = \frac{49}{6}.
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## Variation Between Risk Groups

The conditional means are

$$
\frac32,\qquad 3,\qquad \frac{11}{2},
$$

with overall mean $\frac{10}{3}$.

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(E[X\mid Y])
&=\frac13\left[
\left(\frac32-\frac{10}{3}\right)^2
+\left(3-\frac{10}{3}\right)^2
+\left(\frac{11}{2}-\frac{10}{3}\right)^2
\right]\\
&=\frac{49}{18}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This measures the variation in average claim amounts **between risk groups**.

---

## Verify the Total Variance

The law of total variance gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(X)
&=E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]
+\operatorname{Var}(E[X\mid Y])\\
&=\frac{49}{6}+\frac{49}{18}=\frac{98}{9}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the conditional calculation agrees with the direct calculation.

::: {.callout-note}

## Interpretation

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=
\underbrace{E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)]}_{\text{within-group variation}}
+
\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(E[X\mid Y])}_{\text{between-group variation}}
}
$$

Total uncertainty consists of variation **within** risk groups and variation **between** their average claim amounts.
:::

---

## Application to the Collective Risk Model

Consider the aggregate claim amount

$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i.
$$

Conditioning on the number of claims $N=n$ gives

$$
S\mid(N=n)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i.
$$

If the claim amounts are iid with

$$
E[X_i]=\mu_X,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma_X^2,
$$

then $\boxed{E[S\mid N=n]=n\mu_X}.$

---

## Application to the Collective Risk Model

Since the claim amounts are independent,

$$
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(S\mid N=n)=n\sigma_X^2}.
$$

Thus, conditional on $N=n$, the aggregate claim amount has

$$
E[S\mid N=n]=n\mu_X,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(S\mid N=n)=n\sigma_X^2.
$$

These results provide the starting point for deriving the moments of the collective risk model.

---

## From Conditional to Unconditional Moments

Using the law of total expectation,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[S]
&=E[E[S\mid N]]\\
&=E[N\mu_X]\\
&=\mu_XE[N].
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the law of total variance,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(S)
&=E[\operatorname{Var}(S\mid N)]
+\operatorname{Var}(E[S\mid N])\\
&=E[N\sigma_X^2]
+\operatorname{Var}(N\mu_X).
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(S)
=
\sigma_X^2E[N]
+\mu_X^2\operatorname{Var}(N)
}.
$$














# Moments of the Collective Risk Model {#moments-collective-risk-model}

## General Setup

Recall the collective risk model

$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i,
$$

where $N$ is the number of claims and $X_i$ is the amount of the $i$th claim.

Assume

$$
X_1,X_2,\ldots \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} F_X,
\qquad
N\perp\!\!\!\perp (X_1,X_2,\ldots).
$$

We derive the moments of $S$ by **conditioning on $N$**.

Let

$$
\mu_X=E[X_1],
\qquad
\sigma_X^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1).
$$

---

## Mean of the Aggregate Loss

Conditional on $N=n$, $S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i.$

Therefore,

$$
E[S\mid N=n]
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}E[X_i]
=
n\mu_X.
$$

Using the law of total expectation,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[S]
&=E[E[S\mid N]]=E[N\mu_X]=\mu_XE[N].
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
E[S]=E[N]E[X_1]
}.
$$

---

## Interpretation of the Mean

The result

$$
\boxed{E[S]=E[N]E[X_1]}
$$

has a simple interpretation:

$$
\text{Expected aggregate claims}
=
\text{Expected number of claims}
\times
\text{Expected claim amount}.
$$

For example, if

$$
E[N]=100
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
E[X_1]=5{,}000,
$$

then

$$
E[S]=100(5{,}000)=500{,}000.
$$

---

## Variance of the Aggregate Loss

Let

$$
m_1=E[X_1],
\qquad
m_2=E[X_1^2].
$$

Then

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=m_2-m_1^2.
$$

Conditional on $N=n$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(S\mid N=n)
=
n\operatorname{Var}(X_1).
$$

Also,

$$
E[S\mid N=n]=nm_1.
$$

---

## Deriving the Variance

By the law of total variance,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(S)
&=E[\operatorname{Var}(S\mid N)]
+\operatorname{Var}(E[S\mid N])\\
&=E[N\operatorname{Var}(X_1)]
+\operatorname{Var}(Nm_1).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $m_1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$ are constants,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(S)
=
E[N]\operatorname{Var}(X_1)
+
\operatorname{Var}(N)(E[X_1])^2
}.
$$

---

## Interpretation of the Variance

The variance decomposes into two sources:

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(S)
=
\underbrace{E[N]\operatorname{Var}(X_1)}
_{\text{claim severity variation}}
+
\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(N)(E[X_1])^2}
_{\text{claim frequency variation}}
}
$$

* The first term arises from variation in individual claim amounts.
* The second term arises because the number of claims is random.

Thus, both **severity uncertainty** and **frequency uncertainty** contribute to aggregate risk.

---

## Third Central Moment

To study skewness, define

$$
\mu_X=E[X_1],
\qquad
\sigma_X^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1),
$$

and

$$
\mu_{3,X}
=
E[(X_1-\mu_X)^3].
$$

For the claim frequency $N$, define

$$
\mu_N=E[N],
\qquad
\sigma_N^2=\operatorname{Var}(N),
$$

and

$$
\mu_{3,N}
=
E[(N-\mu_N)^3].
$$

---

## Third Central Moment of $S$

For the random sum

$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i,
$$

the third central moment is

$$
\boxed{
\mu_{3,S}
=
\mu_N\mu_{3,X}
+
3\sigma_N^2\mu_X\sigma_X^2
+
\mu_{3,N}\mu_X^3
}.
$$

The three terms have distinct sources:

1. individual claim severity;
2. interaction between frequency and severity variation;
3. skewness of the claim frequency.

---

## Coefficient of Skewness

For a random variable $X$, the coefficient of skewness is

$$
\gamma_1
=
\frac{E[(X-E[X])^3]}
{\operatorname{Var}(X)^{3/2}}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\gamma_{1,S}
=
\frac{\mu_{3,S}}
{\operatorname{Var}(S)^{3/2}}
}.
$$

Substituting the collective risk model moments gives

$$
\boxed{
\gamma_{1,S}
=
\frac{
\mu_N\mu_{3,X}
+
3\sigma_N^2\mu_X\sigma_X^2
+
\mu_{3,N}\mu_X^3
}{
\left(
\mu_N\sigma_X^2+\sigma_N^2\mu_X^2
\right)^{3/2}
}
}.
$$

---

## Summary of the First Three Moments

For $S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i$, define

$$
\mu_N=E[N],\qquad
\sigma_N^2=\operatorname{Var}(N),\qquad
\mu_{3,N}=E[(N-\mu_N)^3].
$$

and

$$
\mu_X=E[X_1],\qquad
\sigma_X^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1),\qquad
\mu_{3,X}=E[(X_1-\mu_X)^3].
$$

Then the first moment is

$$
\boxed{E[S]=\mu_N\mu_X}.
$$

---

## Summary of the First Three Moments

The variance is

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}(S)
=
\mu_N\sigma_X^2+\sigma_N^2\mu_X^2
}.
$$

The third central moment is

$$
\boxed{
\mu_{3,S}
=
\mu_N\mu_{3,X}
+
3\sigma_N^2\mu_X\sigma_X^2
+
\mu_{3,N}\mu_X^3
}.
$$

---

## Reading the Moment Formulas

The collective risk model combines two random quantities:

$$
\boxed{
N
\quad\text{and}\quad
X_1,X_2,\ldots
}
$$

The aggregate moments therefore depend on moments of **both frequency and severity**.

| Aggregate quantity      | Depends on                                                       |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| $E[S]$                  | $E[N]$, $E[X]$                                                   |
| $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ | $E[N]$, $\operatorname{Var}(N)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, $E[X]$ |
| $\mu_{3,S}$             | first three moments of $N$ and $X$                               |

This allows different frequency distributions to be compared while keeping the same severity model.

---

## Moment Generating Function

The random-sum representation also gives a general formula for the MGF.

Let

$$
M_X(t)=E[e^{tX_1}],
\qquad
M_N(t)=E[e^{tN}].
$$

Conditional on $N=n$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[e^{tS}\mid N=n]
&=
E\left[
e^{t(X_1+\cdots+X_n)}
\right]\\
&=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}E[e^{tX_i}]\\
&=
\left(M_X(t)\right)^n.
\end{aligned}
$$

The independence of the claim amounts is used here.

---

## Deriving the Aggregate MGF

Since

$$
E[e^{tS}\mid N]
=
\left(M_X(t)\right)^N,
$$

the law of total expectation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_S(t)
&=E[e^{tS}]\\
&=E\left[\left(M_X(t)\right)^N\right]\\
&=E\left[
e^{N\log(M_X(t))}
\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of $M_N$,

$$
\boxed{
M_S(t)
=
M_N\left(\log M_X(t)\right)
}.
$$

This is the general MGF formula for the collective risk model.

---

## Using the Aggregate MGF

The formula

$$
\boxed{
M_S(t)=M_N\left(\log M_X(t)\right)
}
$$

means that the aggregate MGF can be obtained from:

* the MGF of the claim severity, $M_X(t)$; and
* the MGF of the claim frequency, $M_N(t)$.

Once these two MGFs are known, substitute

$$
t\longmapsto \log M_X(t)
$$

into $M_N(t)$.

This provides another route to the moments of $S$.

---

## From General to Special Models

The general results apply to any claim frequency distribution for which the required moments exist.

Important cases include:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ccc}
N &\longrightarrow& S\\[2pt]
\text{Binomial}
&\longrightarrow&
\text{Compound Binomial}\\
\text{Poisson}
&\longrightarrow&
\text{Compound Poisson}\\
\text{Negative binomial}
&\longrightarrow&
\text{Compound Negative Binomial}
\end{array}
}
$$

The next section considers these **special compound distributions** and their properties.








# Special Compound Distributions {#special-compound-distributions}

## Compound Poisson Distribution

Suppose the claim frequency follows a Poisson distribution:

$$
N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda).
$$

Assume the claim severities are iid and independent of $N$:

$$
X_1,X_2,\ldots\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}F_X.
$$

The aggregate claim amount is

$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i.
$$

Then $S$ has a **compound Poisson distribution**, written as $\boxed{S\sim\mathcal{CP}(\lambda,F_X)}.$

---

## Compound Poisson Model

The compound Poisson model combines:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\\
X_i\sim F_X
\end{array}
}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{
S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i
}
$$

Here,

* $\lambda$ is the expected number of claims;
* $F_X$ is the severity distribution;
* $S$ is the aggregate claim amount.

Thus, the Poisson distribution models **frequency**, while $F_X$ models **severity**.

---

## Moments of the Compound Poisson Model

Let $m_k=E[X_1^k]$ denote the $k$th raw moment of the claim severity.

For

$$
N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda),
$$

we have

$$
E[N]=\operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,
$$

$$
\mu_{3,N}
=
E[(N-E[N])^3]
=
\lambda.
$$

These quantities can be substituted into the general collective risk formulas.

---

## Mean

For the collective risk model,

$$
E[S]=E[N]E[X_1].
$$

Since

$$
E[N]=\lambda
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
E[X_1]=m_1,
$$

we obtain

$$
\boxed{E[S]=\lambda m_1}.
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
\text{Expected aggregate claims}
=
\text{expected frequency}
\times
\text{expected severity}
}.
$$

---

## Variance

The general variance formula is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(S)
=
E[N]\operatorname{Var}(X_1)
+
\operatorname{Var}(N)(E[X_1])^2.
$$

For the Poisson frequency model,

$$
E[N]=\operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(S)
&=\lambda(m_2-m_1^2)+\lambda m_1^2=\lambda m_2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(S)=\lambda m_2}.$

---

## A Useful Compound Poisson Result

For

$$
S\sim\mathcal{CP}(\lambda,F_X),
$$

the first two moments are particularly simple:

$$
\boxed{
E[S]=\lambda m_1,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(S)=\lambda m_2.
}
$$

The variance depends on the **second raw moment** of the claim severity, rather than only on its variance.

This property is specific to the Poisson frequency model.

---

## MGF of the Compound Poisson Model

The general random-sum MGF formula is

$$
M_S(t)
=
M_N\left(\log M_X(t)\right).
$$

For a Poisson random variable,

$$
M_N(t)=\exp\{\lambda(e^t-1)\}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_S(t)
&=
\exp\left\{
\lambda\left(
e^{\log M_X(t)}-1
\right)
\right\}=
\exp\{\lambda(M_X(t)-1)\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
M_S(t)=\exp\{\lambda(M_X(t)-1)\}
}.
$$

---

## Third Central Moment

For the collective risk model,

$$
\mu_{3,S}
=
E[N]\mu_{3,X}
+
3\operatorname{Var}(N)\mu_X\sigma_X^2
+
\mu_{3,N}\mu_X^3.
$$

For a Poisson frequency distribution,

$$
E[N]=\operatorname{Var}(N)=\mu_{3,N}=\lambda.
$$

Thus,

$$
\mu_{3,S}
=
\lambda
\left[
\mu_{3,X}
+3\mu_X\sigma_X^2
+\mu_X^3
\right].
$$

Using $\mu_{3,X}=m_3-3m_1m_2+2m_1^3,$ we obtain

$$
\boxed{\mu_{3,S}=\lambda m_3}.
$$

---

## Coefficient of Skewness

The coefficient of skewness is

$$
\operatorname{Sk}(S)
=
\frac{\mu_{3,S}}
{\operatorname{Var}(S)^{3/2}}.
$$

For the compound Poisson model, $\mu_{3,S}=\lambda m_3\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{Var}(S)=\lambda m_2.$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Sk}(S)
=
\frac{\lambda m_3}
{(\lambda m_2)^{3/2}}
}
$$

or equivalently,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Sk}(S)
=
\frac{m_3}
{\sqrt{\lambda}\,m_2^{3/2}}
}.
$$

---

## First Three Cumulants

The first three cumulants of a compound Poisson random variable have a useful form:

$$
\boxed{
\kappa_r(S)=\lambda E[X^r],
\qquad r=1,2,3.
}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\kappa_1(S)=\lambda m_1,
\qquad
\kappa_2(S)=\lambda m_2,
\qquad
\kappa_3(S)=\lambda m_3.
}
$$

Since

$$
\kappa_1=E[S],
\qquad
\kappa_2=\operatorname{Var}(S),
$$

this immediately gives the first two moment results.

---

## Compound Poisson Moments: Summary

For

$$
S\sim\mathcal{CP}(\lambda,F_X),
$$

with $m_k=E[X^k]$, the first three moments are

$$
\boxed{E[S]=\lambda m_1},
\qquad
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(S)=\lambda m_2},
\qquad
\boxed{\mu_{3,S}=\lambda m_3}.
$$

---

## Compound Poisson Moments: Summary

The skewness is

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Sk}(S)
=
\frac{m_3}{\sqrt{\lambda}\,m_2^{3/2}}
}.
$$

The MGF is

$$
\boxed{
M_S(t)=\exp\{\lambda(M_X(t)-1)\}.
}
$$

---

## Worked Example: Compound Poisson-Pareto Model

Suppose

$$
S\sim\mathcal{CP}(10,F_X),
$$

where

$$
X\sim\operatorname{Pa}(4,1).
$$

Calculate $E[S],\qquad\operatorname{Var}(S),\qquad\operatorname{Sk}(S).$

For a Pareto distribution with shape $\alpha=4$ and scale $\beta=1$,

$$
E[X^r]
=
\frac{\alpha\beta^r}{\alpha-r},
\qquad r<\alpha.
$$

---

## Pareto Severity Moments

For $\alpha=4$ and $\beta=1$, the raw moments under the parameterisation

$$
f_X(x)=\frac{\alpha\beta^\alpha}{x^{\alpha+1}},
\qquad x\geq\beta,
$$

are

$$
\boxed{
E[X^r]=\frac{\alpha\beta^r}{\alpha-r},
\qquad r<\alpha.
}
$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{m_1=E[X]=\frac43}.
$$

---

## Pareto Severity Moments

For $\alpha=4$ and $\beta=1$,

$$
\boxed{
m_1=\frac43,
\qquad
m_2=2,
\qquad
m_3=4.
}
$$

In particular, $m_3$ exists because the condition $r<\alpha$ is satisfied for $r=3$.

---

## Pareto Parameterisation

The values above depend on the Pareto parameterisation.

Under the `actuar` parameterisation,

$$
X\sim\operatorname{Pa}(4,1),
$$

with survival function

$$
P(X>x)=\left(\frac{1}{1+x}\right)^4,
\qquad x>0,
$$

the raw moments are

$$
\boxed{
m_1=\frac13,
\qquad
m_2=\frac13,
\qquad
m_3=1.
}
$$

---

## Pareto Parameterisation

The numerical example below uses **this parameterisation**, consistent with the original calculation.

Thus, throughout the example,

$$
\boxed{
m_1=\frac13,\qquad
m_2=\frac13,\qquad
m_3=1.
}
$$


---

## Compound Poisson-Pareto Example

For the specified parameterisation,

$$
\lambda=10,
\qquad
m_1=\frac13,
\qquad
m_2=\frac13,
\qquad
m_3=1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[S]
&=\lambda m_1
=10\left(\frac13\right)
=\frac{10}{3},\\
\operatorname{Var}(S)
&=\lambda m_2
=10\left(\frac13\right)
=\frac{10}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## Compound Poisson-Pareto Skewness

Using

$$
\operatorname{Sk}(S)
=
\frac{\lambda m_3}
{(\lambda m_2)^{3/2}},
$$

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Sk}(S)
&=
\frac{10}
{(10/3)^{3/2}}\approx1.6432.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
E[S]=\frac{10}{3},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(S)=\frac{10}{3},
\qquad
\operatorname{Sk}(S)\approx1.6432.
}
$$

The positive skewness reflects the right-skewed, heavy-tailed severity distribution.

---

## Simulating a Compound Poisson Model

To simulate one aggregate loss:

1. Simulate the number of claims:

   $$
   N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda).
   $$

2. Simulate $N$ claim amounts:

   $$
   X_1,\ldots,X_N\sim F_X.
   $$

3. Add the claim amounts:

   $$
   S=X_1+\cdots+X_N.
   $$

Repeating these steps gives a sample from the aggregate loss distribution.

---

## R Simulation

```r
library(actuar)

n <- 10000; lambda <- 10; alpha <- 4; beta <- 1

numclaims <- rpois(n, lambda); totalClaims <- numeric(n)

for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  totalClaims[i] <- sum(
    rpareto(numclaims[i], shape = alpha, scale = beta
    )
  )
}
```


```{r}
library(actuar)

n <- 10000
lambda <- 10
alpha <- 4
beta <- 1

numclaims <- rpois(n, lambda)

totalClaims <- numeric(n)

for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  totalClaims[i] <- sum(
    rpareto(
      numclaims[i],
      shape = alpha,
      scale = beta
    )
  )
}
```

Each element of `totalClaims` is one simulated aggregate claim amount.

---

## Simulated Aggregate Claims

```{r}
hist(
  totalClaims,
  breaks = 50,
  main = "Simulated Compound Poisson Aggregate Claims",
  xlab = "Aggregate claim amount"
)
```

The simulation produces an empirical distribution of

$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i.
$$

With a sufficiently large simulation sample, the empirical moments should be close to their theoretical values.

---

## Simulation versus Theory

The theoretical values are

$$
E[S]=\frac{10}{3},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(S)=\frac{10}{3},
\qquad
\operatorname{Sk}(S)\approx1.6432.
$$

The sample estimates will not be exactly equal to these values because the simulation contains only a finite number of observations.

As the number of simulations increases, the sample estimates should generally become closer to the theoretical values.

---

## Additivity of Compound Poisson Risks

Suppose

$$
S_i\sim\mathcal{CP}(\lambda_i,F_i),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,
$$

are independent, and let

$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}S_i.
$$

Then $S$ is also compound Poisson:

$$
\boxed{S\sim\mathcal{CP}(\lambda,F)}.
$$

---

## Additivity of Compound Poisson Risks

The aggregate Poisson parameter is

$$
\boxed{\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i},
$$

while the severity distribution is the weighted mixture

$$
\boxed{
F(x)=\frac{1}{\lambda}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_iF_i(x).
}
$$

Thus, the combined risk has **total claim frequency** $\lambda$ and a **frequency-weighted severity distribution** $F$.

---

## Why Is the Severity Distribution a Mixture?

The aggregate number of claims is Poisson with parameter

$$
\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i.
$$

A claim in the combined portfolio comes from component $i$ with probability

$$
\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda}.
$$

Therefore, the severity distribution of a randomly selected claim is the weighted mixture

$$
F(x)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda}F_i(x).
$$

---

## Why Is the Severity Distribution a Mixture?

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
F(x)
=
\frac{1}{\lambda}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_iF_i(x).
}
$$

The weights are proportional to the claim frequencies $\lambda_i$. A component with a higher claim frequency contributes a larger proportion of claims to the combined portfolio.


---

## Example: Additivity

Suppose two independent portfolios have aggregate losses

$$
S_1\sim\mathcal{CP}(100,F_1),
\qquad
S_2\sim\mathcal{CP}(50,F_2).
$$

Then

$$
S=S_1+S_2
$$

has a compound Poisson distribution with

$$
\boxed{\lambda=100+50=150}.
$$

---

## Example: Additivity

The severity distribution is the frequency-weighted mixture

$$
\boxed{
F(x)
=
\frac{100}{150}F_1(x)
+
\frac{50}{150}F_2(x)
}.
$$

Thus, independent compound Poisson portfolios can be combined into a single compound Poisson model.


---

## Special Compound Distributions

The collective risk model becomes a specific compound distribution when a frequency distribution is chosen.

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ccc}
N & & S\\[2pt]
\text{Poisson}
&\longrightarrow&
\text{Compound Poisson}\\
\text{Binomial}
&\longrightarrow&
\text{Compound Binomial}\\
\text{Negative binomial}
&\longrightarrow&
\text{Compound Negative Binomial}
\end{array}
}
$$

The **compound Poisson model** is particularly useful because it has simple moment and MGF formulas and is closed under addition of independent risks.

---

## Special Compound Distributions

::: {.callout-note}

## Key results

For

$$
S\sim\mathcal{CP}(\lambda,F_X),
$$

the main formulas are

$$
E[S]=\lambda m_1,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(S)=\lambda m_2,
$$

$$
\mu_{3,S}=\lambda m_3,
\qquad
M_S(t)=\exp\{\lambda(M_X(t)-1)\}.
$$

These formulas will be used repeatedly in aggregate risk modelling.
:::
